chapters.title: Make Them Want to Follow You: The Law of Fickleness

chapterBreakdown.gentle: The chapter on fickleness and authority stays useful because it names a pattern people often feel before they can explain it. This law argues that people are fickle in what they demand from leaders, so authority has to be established through steadiness, fairness, anti-neediness, and inner authority rather than entitlement. Entitlement is the poison. Once a leader assumes loyalty is owed, sensitivity to fairness and emotional climate drops. Authority starts reading as appetite rather than service. Respect erodes, and people begin to test, withdraw, or wait for failure. The practical move is to build inner authority first: emotional steadiness, self-command, consistency, fairness, and a visible willingness to carry burden. When people sense that you are not feeding on the role, followership becomes less reluctant and more willing. Authority lasts when it looks steady and fair rather than hungry. That softer honesty is already a practical advantage.

Followers can ask for strong leadership and then immediately start testing, resenting, or undermining it, which makes authority one of the least stable and most emotionally loaded forms of power. Greene treats fickleness as a predictable instability in human followership. People want safety, clarity, and competence, but they also resist feeling small, controlled, or taken for granted. That tension makes leadership fragile when it leans only on title or force. Entitlement is the poison. Once a leader assumes loyalty is owed, sensitivity to fairness and emotional climate drops.
